newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition drops demos, urges free media.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition drops demos, urges free media.

text.p: The Serbian opposition said on Saturday they would suspend marathon street protests for three weeks to give the government time to meet their demands for liberalising the state-run media.

Zoran Djindjic, co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, told demonstrators on the 88th day of street protests: "Let us give them a chance to show an intention to free the media and, if they fail to do that by March 9, then what else can we do but go out into the streets again."

Djindjic told around 10,000 demonstrators in central Belgrade -- a fraction of the 500,000 that took to the streets at the height of the protests -- that they had achieved one of their main aims, the recognition of opposition gains in local elections, but that two key goals remained.

"Our three objectives were to get back our election victory, and achieve the deblocking of the media and fair conditions ahead of the next elections. We have achieved the first, but not the other two."
"We shall give them three weeks, until March 9 -- let us see what will happen by March 9."
"After the media are freed, we shall talk about fair conditions for the elections, and a new election-financing law," he said.

Zajedno launched the protests after the authoritarian government of President Slobodan Milosevic annulled opposition victories in 14 major Serbian cities, including Belgrade, in local elections last November.
Earlier this week the government caved in to pressure from the streets and from abroad and introduced a special law recognising the poll gains.

However the opposition has made it clear they are also seeking wide-ranging reforms of Serbia's centralised system, with general elections looming later this year, in particular a liberalisation of the state television and radio used by Milosevic to help keep him in power.
"All our institutions are only an instrument for preserving the regime, and that is why we must persevere in the struggle to achieve our aims," Djindjic told the crowd.

"Serbia is like a man half-way down in quicksand -- he cannot stay there for ever, he must either get out or sink and die -- we must continue our struggle in order to protect the elementary right we have won, the right to our dignity."
Opposition leaders announced they would hold a celebration party on Friday to mark the first session of the opposition-led local council in Belgrade.

Belgrade students who have been also been demonstrating for nearly three months said they would continue their protests until the government met their demands for the sacking of the university rector and his deputy and the prosecution of those responsible for annulling the local elections.

A student leader told Reuters on Saturday that since the government had recognised the opposition election gains they would consider resuming their studies if the two university officials were replaced.
